title: US Rep proposes bill to give video game buyers "ownership," not "a license"
gist: Rep. Ritchie Torres (D-NY) has proposed the Power to Players Act, directing the FTC to make game purchases confer ownership rather than revocable licenses, including requiring offline modes for online-only games like NBA 2K25, which goes dark December 31. Ars Technica places it within a preservation push amid Sony's 82% digital share, while noting technical feasibility doubts, unclear prospects, and AI-enabled decompilation as a wildcard.

themes.theme: Power to the Players Act: purchase as ownership

insights.claim: Rep. Ritchie Torres (D-NY) has proposed the Power to Players Act, which directs the FTC to ensure that buying a video game confers ownership rather than a revocable license to play it.
insights.speaker: Samuel Axon
insights.so_what: Potential US regulation could constrain publishers' ability to end support for sold games, raising long-tail obligations and costs.
insights.locator: A new bill proposed by Rep.

insights.claim: The bill's announcement cites NBA 2K25, which launched September 6, 2025, and is scheduled to become unplayable on December 31 because of server shutdowns, as the kind of outcome it aims to prevent.
insights.speaker: Samuel Axon
insights.so_what: Annual sports titles with short server lifespans are the most exposed business model if the bill advances.

insights.claim: Torres argues that a game that can be revoked when a company pulls the plug is a rental disguised as a sale, and that consumers should have the right to own, play, and transfer games they buy.
insights.speaker: Ritchie Torres
insights.so_what: A transfer right could revive resale markets and pressure digital storefront economics.
insights.quote: A game that can be taken away the moment a company pulls the plug is not a purchase. It is a rental disguised as a sale.

insights.claim: Torres frames the bill's proposed status quo as a restoration of the historical norm of game ownership players experienced in the 1990s.
insights.speaker: Ritchie Torres
insights.so_what: Positions the policy as consumer-protection restoration, which may broaden its political appeal.
insights.quote: “I think there should be a simple rule: if you pay for it, you own it,” Torres told Kotaku.

insights.claim: Sony reported that digital downloads accounted for 82 percent of full-game unit sales across PlayStation 4 and PlayStation 5 in its covered fiscal year, implying under 20 percent of games are bought on physical media.
insights.speaker: Samuel Axon
insights.so_what: Confirms console game distribution is overwhelmingly digital, concentrating margin with platform storefronts.
insights.quote: Sony revealed that digital downloads account for 82 percent of full-game unit sales across PlayStation 4 and PlayStation 5

insights.claim: Some consumers are protesting Sony's plan to discontinue releases of PlayStation games on physical media, arguing physical discs aid long-term preservation of games that get delisted from digital marketplaces.
insights.speaker: Samuel Axon
insights.so_what: Consumer backlash is a reputational and policy risk to platform holders moving to all-digital.

insights.claim: Physical discs do not by themselves solve preservation, because many disc games still require online servers and EULAs state buyers get a revocable license, while patches often make the disc version meaningfully different from the version players know.
insights.speaker: Samuel Axon
insights.so_what: Format alone does not protect consumers, which is why pressure is shifting toward legislation on industry practices.
insights.quote: the end-user license agreements make it clear that the user is purchasing a revocable license, not actual ownership of the media
insights.locator: Physical discs don’t solve the problem

insights.claim: Activist and lobbying movements such as Stop Killing Games have pushed for change, but proposed bills around the world have suggested different kinds of solutions.
insights.speaker: Samuel Axon
insights.so_what: A fragmented global regulatory landscape could raise compliance complexity for game publishers.

themes.theme: Feasibility and outlook of the legislation

insights.claim: Unlike prior proposals criticized for requiring servers to run indefinitely, the Torres bill as described would instead require normally online-only games to offer offline modes so players can keep playing after server shutdowns.
insights.speaker: Samuel Axon
insights.so_what: Mandated offline modes could force costly architectural changes for live-service game developers.

insights.claim: Because of how some online games are engineered, mandatory offline modes may not be feasible and could require developers to take very different approaches to online game architecture.
insights.speaker: Samuel Axon
insights.so_what: Live-service titles face potential redesign costs and industry resistance if such rules pass.

insights.claim: The Power to Players Act's passage is uncertain: most proposed legislation never reaches a vote, and the bill's full text is not yet public, so its effectiveness and enforceability cannot be assessed.
insights.speaker: Samuel Axon
insights.so_what: Near-term regulatory impact on game publishers is low-probability; treat it as a headline risk rather than a base case.
insights.quote: most proposed legislation never even makes it to a vote

insights.claim: Large language models and specialized coding harnesses have enabled a wave of decompilations and reconfigurations of classic and contemporary games, which are likely illegal but may be hard to enforce against at scale and could reshape software preservation.
insights.speaker: Samuel Axon
insights.so_what: AI-driven decompilation could erode publishers' control over their back catalogs regardless of legislation.
insights.quote: These projects are almost certainly currently illegal, but the scale of the movement is such that enforcement may be difficult.
